governanceNotes: D1 batch 44 (2026-09-24): one bounded association edge authored - hemorrhoids to anemia (rank 1), ASSOCIATION_ONLY with etiologicalConsensus NOT_ESTABLISHED, vaNexusProbabilityAlignment NOT_ASSERTED, hypothesizedOnly:true, and mechanismCategory THROMBOTIC_OR_VASCULAR (hemorrhoidal vascular-cushion bleeding). The proposition rests on two independent clinical anchors: the Deng 2024 retrospective study of 128 patients with hemorrhoidal severe anemia, which quantifies preoperative transfusion requirements, transfusion reactions, and hospitalization burden in that population, and the Dong 2025 case report of mixed hemorrhoids with severe anemia in which sclerotherapy was used for the anemia-related presentation - a severity-and-dechallenge-flavored case anchor. The edge is not raised to causation: the located evidence documents that hemorrhoidal bleeding can produce clinically severe anemia and quantifies treatment burden, but no cohort quantifies incident anemia attributable to hemorrhoids against matched controls, chronic bleeding is frequently multifactorial in the same populations, and competing gastrointestinal and systemic causes of anemia must be excluded per case, so no probability estimate is asserted.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Clinical reports and a single-center retrospective series document that hemorrhoidal bleeding can produce severe anemia requiring transfusion: the Deng 2024 study of 128 patients with hemorrhoidal severe anemia quantifies preoperative transfusion requirements, transfusion reactions, and hospitalization burden, and the Dong 2025 case report describes mixed hemorrhoids presenting with severe anemia managed by sclerotherapy - a reproducible bleeding-to-anemia association that is not an individual causal nexus.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established: the located evidence is case-level plus one single-center retrospective series without matched comparators, anemia in these populations is frequently multifactorial, and other gastrointestinal (ulcer, malignancy, angiodysplasia, inflammatory bowel disease, medication-related) and non-gastrointestinal causes of anemia must be excluded, so an individual determination requires a documented hemorrhoidal bleeding source, blood counts and iron studies with compatible chronology, and competing-cause review.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized bleeding-to-depletion route is described: repeated bleeding from engorged hemorrhoidal vascular cushions produces chronic blood loss that depletes iron stores faster than absorption can replace them, and if bleeding continues the marrow cannot maintain hemoglobin, producing microcytic iron-deficiency anemia that can become severe enough to require transfusion - documented in the located case report and the 128-patient transfusion series - while the absence of matched-cohort incidence data and the multifactorial anemia context leave individual attribution hypothesized.
causalMechanism.secondaryVector: Acute bleeding from thrombosed or ulcerated hemorrhoidal tissue can produce faster hemoglobin decline, and coexisting anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy can amplify blood loss in the same patients.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: The edge asserts an association only: the located evidence is one case report and one single-center retrospective series of transfusion-requiring hemorrhoidal anemia, without matched-cohort incidence data, and anemia in the reported populations is frequently multifactorial with competing gastrointestinal and systemic causes requiring exclusion, so no at-least-as-likely-as-not probability is asserted.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Documentation of hemorrhoidal disease with bleeding (grade, examination or endoscopic findings, date); serial blood counts and iron studies with chronology relative to the bleeding; documentation of the bleeding source and exclusion of other gastrointestinal sources (ulcer, malignancy, angiodysplasia, inflammatory bowel disease, medication-related mucosal injury); assessment of anticoagulant, antiplatelet, or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory use; evaluation for non-gastrointestinal anemia causes (renal, hematologic, nutritional, chronic inflammatory); transfusion history and response to hemorrhoid-directed treatment; gastroenterology or hematology assessment of the individual relationship
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Peptic ulcer or other upper gastrointestinal bleeding source
Angiodysplasia or other lower gastrointestinal vascular lesion
Inflammatory bowel disease or medication-related mucosal injury
Nutritional, renal, hematologic, or chronic-inflammatory anemia

suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY: a 128-patient single-center series and a case report document hemorrhoidal severe anemia and its transfusion burden, establishing that hemorrhoidal bleeding can produce clinically significant blood loss, but no matched-cohort incidence data exist and competing gastrointestinal and systemic causes of anemia are common in the same populations, so the consensus remains NOT_ESTABLISHED with source-documentation, chronology, and competing-cause requirements; no probability estimate is asserted.
